findings.title: Silent resolution of multiple CryptoProviders removes a fail-fast safety check
findings.body: Previously, detectProvider() threw an IllegalStateException if more than one CryptoProvider was found on the classloader, forcing operators to fix a misconfigured classpath (e.g. accidentally shipping both DefaultCryptoProvider and FIPS1402Provider together). The new code silently keeps only the highest-order provider and logs the ignored ones at debug level only (logger.debugf), which is typically disabled in production. All three built-in providers (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider) use the same order()=200, so if two of them end up on the same classpath by mistake, selection among ties depends on ServiceLoader iteration order (jar/classpath ordering), which is not guaranteed to be deterministic across environments. For FIPS-sensitive deployments this can silently select a non-FIPS-compliant provider instead of failing loudly as before, which is a meaningful regression in safety/compliance guarantees without any visible warning.

findings.title: New abstract method order() breaks binary/source compatibility for existing implementers
findings.body: CryptoProvider is a public SPI interface loaded via ServiceLoader; adding a new abstract method order() (without a default implementation) means any existing third-party or external implementation of CryptoProvider will fail to compile/implement the interface until updated. All in-repo implementers were updated in this PR, but any external module implementing this interface (which is exactly the scenario this PR is designed to support, e.g. authz-client) will break unless it also adds order(). A default method (e.g. returning a baseline value) would preserve compatibility while still allowing providers to opt into custom ordering.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider() does not return a BouncyCastle provider, violating the interface contract
findings.body: CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider() is documented as returning "BouncyCastle security provider. Can be either non-FIPS or FIPS based provider". This implementation instead returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is simply whatever JCA provider backs the JVM's default keystore type (e.g. SUN/SunJSSE for 'pkcs12' or 'jks'), unrelated to BouncyCastle. Any shared keycloak-core code path that calls this method expecting an actual BC(-FIPS) provider (e.g. to perform signature/key operations that require BC-specific algorithm support) will silently get the wrong provider instead of a clear failure, which can cause subtle incorrect behavior rather than an explicit error.

findings.title: Dead code in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
findings.body: In concatenatedRSToASN1DER, the lines `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` create two throwaway ASN1Encoder instances, write to them, and discard the result without ever using it. This is leftover/dead code that serves no purpose and should be removed before merge; it suggests the implementation was not fully cleaned up.

findings.title: Inconsistent use of KeystoreFormat.name() instead of toString()
findings.body: getKeyStore() here calls `KeyStore.getInstance(format.name())`, whereas DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all use `format.toString()`. If KeystoreUtil.KeystoreFormat ever overrides toString() to map enum constants to different keystore type strings, this implementation would silently diverge from the other providers and could request the wrong keystore type. Even if currently harmless, it is an inconsistency that should match the pattern used elsewhere in the codebase.

findings.title: No test coverage for the new order()-based provider selection logic
findings.body: This PR's core mechanism change (allowing multiple CryptoProvider instances on the classpath and resolving via order(), replacing the previous exception-on-conflict behavior) has no accompanying unit test. There is no test verifying that the highest-order provider is chosen when multiple providers are present, nor one covering the tie-breaking behavior when providers share the same order value. Given this is a behavior-changing core feature (and a security-relevant one, since it silently resolves what used to be a hard error), it should be covered by dedicated tests in common's test sources.

findings.title: Unconditional CryptoIntegration.init() now exposes a crypto provider with mostly unimplemented operations
findings.body: AuthzClient.create(Configuration) now always calls CryptoIntegration.init(), which, for real consumers of the published org.keycloak:keycloak-authz-client artifact, will typically resolve to AuthzClientCryptoProvider as the only CryptoProvider on the classpath (since it has the lowest order=100 and is meant to be overridden when a full provider like DefaultCryptoProvider is also present, which downstream consumers are unlikely to bundle). That provider throws UnsupportedOperationException for the majority of CryptoProvider methods (getAlgorithmProvider, getCertificateUtils, getPemUtils, getOCSPProver, getIdentityExtractorProvider, createECParams, getKeyPairGen, getKeyFactory, getAesCbcCipher/getAesGcmCipher, getSecretKeyFact, getX509CertFactory, getCertStore, getCertPathBuilder, getSignature, wrapFactoryForTruststore). Any current or future authz-client code path (or shared keycloak-core code invoked by it) that relies on these operations will now fail at runtime with UnsupportedOperationException instead of either working (if it didn't previously touch CryptoIntegration) or failing clearly at startup.

findings.title: Indefinite-length ASN.1 encoding not rejected, silently mis-parses malformed sequences
findings.body: readLength() returns -1 for the BER indefinite-length form (0x80) without raising an error, but DER (which is what ECDSA signatures must use) never permits indefinite length. In readSequence(), the loop condition `while (length > 0)` treats a -1 length as "already done", silently producing an empty element list instead of rejecting the malformed/non-DER input outright. The subsequent `seq.size() != 2` check in AuthzClientCryptoProvider happens to catch this particular case, but the decoder itself does not validate or reject indefinite-length encodings, which is a correctness gap for an ASN.1 DER parser handling externally-supplied signature bytes.
